opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me, it's a real pleasure to be here.

When I was an undergrad studying electrical engineering, wireless communications was one of the hottest areas. There was a lot of exciting theory, and mobile phones and networks were growing quickly, so it felt like a natural thing to study. But the more I learned, the more I wanted to do research rather than just learn the established material. I wanted to be on the side of creating new knowledge.

At that time, if you looked at where the most influential papers, professors, and new ideas were coming from, a lot of it was in the U.S. The American graduate system was also very appealing. A PhD there gives you a lot of freedom. You work closely with an advisor, but you're expected to find your own problems and develop your own taste. That kind of training was hard to find elsewhere.

There was also a practical side. Many U.S. programs offer funding through research or teaching assistantships, so going abroad was financially realistic for a student like me. Many seniors I respected had gone that route, and hearing their stories made it feel achievable rather than distant.

Honestly, part of it was simply curiosity. I wanted to see a bigger world and test myself against very strong people. I didn't know yet that I'd eventually move from communications into computer vision and machine learning. But the U.S. research environment made that kind of shift possible. It's quite open, and if you find a new direction that excites you, people will generally let you pursue it. In hindsight, that flexibility turned out to matter even more than the specific field I started in.

r001.rationale: The candidate says he wanted to create new knowledge and saw influential work coming from the U.S., but it does not describe zero-to-one breakthroughs in contrast with incremental improvements in his wireless research at National Chiao Tung University.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, it wasn't a very dramatic decision at the time. I was doing my undergraduate and master's work in Taiwan, in electrical engineering, and my thesis was on wireless communications, things like channel estimation and signal processing. I liked the math. But when I looked at the people I admired, the ones whose papers I was reading, almost all of them were in the U.S. The labs with the resources, the professors who were defining the field, the companies building the products, they were all there. So going to the U.S. for a PhD felt less like a choice and more like the natural next step if you were serious about research.

The other thing is that in Taiwan at that time, the industry path was very clear. You finish your degree, you go to TSMC or MediaTek, you have a good life. And that's a fine path. But I had this feeling that I didn't yet know what I was good at, and I wanted a few more years to find out. A PhD in the U.S. gave me that room. Nobody expected me to be productive immediately. I could be wrong for a while.

What I didn't expect was that I would switch fields entirely. I went to Maryland for wireless, but during the first year I took a computer vision class, and I realized that the kind of problems that excited me were visual ones. In communications, the signal is well defined. You know what you're trying to recover. In vision, nobody even agrees on what the right representation is. That uncertainty was uncomfortable, but it was also where I felt most alive. My advisor, Rama Chellappa, was generous enough to let me make that jump, and that's really how everything that came later started.

r001.rationale: The candidate says U.S. labs and researchers made a PhD feel like a natural next step, but does not describe seeking “zero-to-one” breakthroughs or contrast them with incremental wireless research at National Chiao Tung University.

astra-6.text: At that point, I was studying wireless communications, and I wanted to go deeper into research—to move beyond learning existing techniques and start asking questions of my own. Graduate study in the U.S. seemed like a good opportunity to do that, to work closely with researchers and explore different directions. I didn’t have my whole career mapped out; I was looking for an environment where I could grow as a researcher.

A lot of the papers we were reading came from universities in the U.S., so graduate school there seemed like a natural way to explore that interest more deeply. I wanted to learn how to do research and see whether it was something I could build a career around.
